conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you were sent in from clinic for severe abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It got really bad again. The pain is all over my stomach, and I feel like I’m going to throw up. I couldn’t handle it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. On a 0 to 10 scale, how bad is the pain right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like an 8. It comes in waves but it’s constant too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. I’ve been nauseous but I haven’t actually thrown up yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to treat your symptoms right away—IV pain medicine and an IV acid-suppressing medication called a proton pump inhibitor. You’re already on pantoprazole by mouth at home; we’ll give a higher-dose IV version here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this the same thing as last time? They said gastritis and ulcers before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your history and how you’re describing it, gastritis—irritation of the stomach lining—can definitely cause this kind of pain and nausea. We’ll also check labs tonight to make sure there’s no sign of infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s something with my tube again. The G-tube is still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I examined your abdomen and the tube site—right now it looks in place. Your belly is tender but soft, which is reassuring. We’ll keep a close eye on it and restart feeds carefully once your symptoms settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for the nausea too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ondansetron through the tube or by mouth is on your home list; we can give it here as needed. Let the nurse know as soon as you feel it building.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds… I don’t want to be knocked out, but I can’t take this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll start with IV pain medication to get you comfortable, then transition you to oral pain medication as soon as you can tolerate it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want this to drag on for weeks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our goal is to get you feeling better quickly and get you home safely. If the IV pantoprazole helps like it has before, that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your initial blood work is back. Your white blood cell count is normal, which is reassuring. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable for you. Kidney function and electrolytes look okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing in the labs suggests an emergency like a major infection. We’ll keep monitoring, but right now this fits best with gastritis-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The IV medicine—how fast should it work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain medicine works quickly. The IV pantoprazole helps reduce acid and irritation; many people feel improvement over hours to a day. We’ll reassess frequently tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now after the IV medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is down to like a 5. Still there, but not as sharp. Nausea is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. If you continue improving, we’ll restart your diet and tube feeds overnight into tomorrow, slowly, and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried eating will set it off again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common concern. We’ll start gently and stop if it worsens. The goal is to keep your nutrition going while we calm the stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m checking in overnight. Any new symptoms—worsening pain, vomiting, dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is more like a 4 now. I’m tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll continue the high-dose IV pantoprazole and keep pain control steady. Try to rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than yesterday. I still feel sore, but I’m not doubled over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your morning labs look stable—kidney function and electrolytes are fine. We’ll continue IV pantoprazole. Today we’re also planning a PICC line placement so you can continue IV pantoprazole at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A PICC line… that’s the long IV, right? Why do I need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a longer IV that sits in a larger vein. Because you’re responding well to the IV pantoprazole and you’ve had recurrent severe symptoms, the plan is to discharge you on IV pantoprazole twice a day at home. A PICC makes that safer and more reliable than regular IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it painful to put in? And is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people feel pressure and a brief pinch, but it’s generally well tolerated. Risks include infection or a clot, but we minimize those with sterile technique and careful care instructions. We’ll confirm the tip position with a chest X-ray afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I still use my G-tube feeds with the PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The PICC is for the IV medication. Your tube feeds and diet plan can continue as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before the PICC team comes, I want to make sure we’re on the same page: we’ll keep your pain controlled, transition fully to oral pain meds, and keep the IV pantoprazole going. How is your pain right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 3. I can talk through it. I’d rather take pills than IV pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect—that’s exactly what we want. We’ll stick with oral pain medication as needed and avoid anything you’re allergic to—no NSAIDs or aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line has been placed. Next step is the chest X-ray to confirm it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My arm feels weird—tight. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness or a tight feeling can happen right after placement. If you notice increasing swelling, redness, fever, or severe pain, tell us right away. We’ll also have home services help you with line care after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back: the PICC tip is in the correct position in the distal SVC, and your lungs look clear—no pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to feel okay on oral pain meds and you’re tolerating your diet and tube feeds. The plan is discharge later today with home IV pantoprazole through the PICC, twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I have to do the IV pantoprazole at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with the medication and refills, and you’ll follow up with Dr. ___ to decide the duration and next steps based on your symptoms and response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds—sucralfate and rifaximin and all that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home regimen: sucralfate four times a day, rifaximin twice a day, and your other usual medications. The main change is pantoprazole will be IV every 12 hours instead of the oral daily dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the PICC get in the way of showering or sleeping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can sleep normally, but avoid pulling on it. For showering, you’ll need to keep the dressing dry—home services will teach you how to cover it and how to watch for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back tonight at home, what do I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your prescribed oral pain medication as directed and your nausea medication if needed. If you have severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting, fever, bleeding, or you can’t tolerate feeds, you should call your surgeon’s office or come back to the emergency department.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge: your pain is controlled on oral meds, you’re tolerating your diet and tube feeds, and the PICC is functioning. Any last questions about the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… is this definitely gastritis? I’m worried we’re missing something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your symptoms, exam, and stable labs—and how well you improved with high-dose IV acid suppression—gastritis is the best explanation for this episode. We’ll keep close follow-up with Dr. ___, and if symptoms change or don’t stay controlled, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything. I’m ready to go home.
